candidate.answerReason: The root sum is (a+b+c+b)/2, which is at most (24+9)/2 = 16.5. The distinct digits a=8, b=9, c=7 attain this bound.

methods.label: Expose the roots and prove an attainable bound
methods.explanation:
Both terms contain \(x-b\), so factoring reveals the roots directly:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(x-a)(x-b)+(x-b)(x-c)\\
&\qquad=(x-b)(2x-a-c).
\end{aligned}
\]
A product is zero exactly when at least one factor is zero. Thus the two roots, counting a repeated root twice if they coincide, are
\[
b\quad\text{and}\quad\frac{a+c}{2}.
\]
Their sum is
\[
S=b+\frac{a+c}{2}
=\frac{a+b+c+b}{2}.
\]
Because the three one-digit numbers are distinct, their sum is at most \(9+8+7=24\). Also, \(b\le9\). Consequently every allowed choice satisfies
\[
S\le\frac{24+9}{2}=16.5.
\]
This bound is attained by \(a=8\), \(b=9\), and \(c=7\): the roots are \(9\) and \(7.5\). Hence the maximum is \(\boxed{16.5}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
methods.levelReason: Common-factor extraction and the zero-product rule give the roots, and elementary bounds on distinct digits establish the maximum.
